title: The BATTLE Trial: A Case Study on Biomarker-Guided, Bayesian Adaptive Trial
text:
The BATTLE Trial: A Case Study on Biomarker-Guided, Bayesian Adaptive Trial How a 255-patient lung-cancer trial made mandatory biopsies, a hierarchical probit model, and outcome-adaptive randomization work in practice — and what it still teaches us about designing modern biomarker-directed trials Author Akif Mustafa Published September 10, 2026 Table of contents Table of contents 1 Introduction 2 Clinical and scientific context (circa 2005) 2.1 The therapeutic plateau BATTLE attacked 2.2 Why a new trial architecture was needed 2.3 Why the 8-week disease-control endpoint 3 The BATTLE program at a glance 4 Inside the design: objectives, biomarker engine, and the Bayesian machinery 4.1 What the trial promised to deliver 4.2 The two-stage architecture 4.3 From 11 biomarkers to 5 marker groups 4.4 The Bayesian hierarchical probit model 4.5 The adaptive-randomization engine 4.6 Futility monitoring: suspension, not execution 5 The biomarker engine: real-time tissue from relapsed lung cancer 5.1 The pipeline, step by step 6 Implementation and operations: where adaptive designs actually live 7 Documented results: what 244 evaluable patients showed 7.1 Patient flow and exposure 7.2 Overall efficacy, and the primary endpoint 7.3 The heart of BATTLE: the arm × marker-group matrix 7.4 Did adaptation actually happen? Yes — visibly 7.5 The individual-marker story the grouping obscured 7.6 Arm postscripts published after the main paper 8 Regulatory interactions, guidance, and the path to acceptance 8.1 What is actually documented about BATTLE and regulators 8.2 Interpretation: what BATTLE did and did not change for regulators 9 Legacy: BATTLE-2 and the platform-trial era 9.1 BATTLE-2: the redesign, honestly reported 9.2 The era BATTLE helped open 10 Ten lessons for designing and analyzing biomarker-guided adaptive trials References 1 Introduction BATTLE-1 offers a rare practical example of adaptive trial design. It was the first completed prospective, biopsy-mandated, biomarker-based, adaptively randomized trial in previously treated non-small-cell lung cancer ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . At MD Anderson Cancer Center, 255 heavily pretreated patients were assigned to four oral targeted therapies using a Bayesian model updated with fresh biopsy biomarkers and 8-week outcomes. ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Zhou et al. 2008 ) . BATTLE is a valuable teaching case for three reasons. First, its design is thoroughly documented , including the statistical model, adaptive-randomization algorithm, futility rules, and operating-characteristic targets ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ; Lee, Gu, and Liu 2010 ) . Second, its operational lessons are as important as its statistics : a multidisciplinary team developed a pipeline to biopsy patients, classify eleven biomarkers, and assign treatment within about two weeks ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Tam et al. 2013 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Third, its limitations are candidly reported , including issues with biomarker grouping, burn-in duration, fragmented eligibility, and population drift ( Liu and Lee 2015 ; Kim et al. 2011 ) . 2 Clinical and scientific context (circa 2005) 2.1 The therapeutic plateau BATTLE attacked By 2005, treatment options for metastatic NSCLC after first-line chemotherapy offered only modest survival gains ( Herbst, Heymach, and Lippman 2008 ) . At the same time, dramatic responses to the EGFR inhibitor gefitinib were observed in selected subgroups, and activating EGFR mutations were identified as the underlying predictor of sensitivity ( Lynch, Bell, and Sordella 2004 ) . The BR.21 trial subsequently showed a modest survival benefit with erlotinib in unselected patients and linked benefit to EGFR mutation status and gene copy number ( M.-S. Tsao, Sakurada, and Cutz 2005 ) . Although the FDA approved erlotinib for previously treated NSCLC in November 2004 without molecular selection ( Cohen, Johnson, and Pazdur 2005 ) , an EGFR companion diagnostic was not approved until May 2013 ( 2013 ) . Thus, when BATTLE was conceived, targeted therapies and predictive biomarkers were available, but prospective biomarker-guided treatment assignment had not yet been implemented in NSCLC ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . 2.2 Why a new trial architecture was needed The trialists at MD Anderson — Edward S. Kim, Roy S. Herbst, Waun Ki Hong, Ignacio Wistuba, and the biostatistics team led by J. Jack Lee — faced a combinatorial problem that classical phase II designs handle poorly ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) : Many agents, many markers. Four targeted agents (erlotinib, vandetanib, erlotinib + bexarotene, sorafenib) each plausibly worked only in marker-defined subgroups. The conventional alternative — 20 separate single-arm studies (4 agents × 5 marker classes) — would be slow, wasteful, and statistically fragile. Unknowable markers in advance. Which biomarker truly predicted benefit was unknown before the trial; a design that locked in subgroup definitions at protocol time risked answering the wrong question. Stale tissue. Biomarkers were usually assessed on archived diagnostic tissue, which may not reflect the biology of a tumor that had relapsed after multiple therapies ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . The BATTLE answer was architectural: one umbrella protocol, four parallel phase II sub-studies, a mandatory fresh biopsy for every patient, prespecified biomarker classes, and a Bayesian engine that reallocated future patients toward treatments performing well in their marker class as outcomes accumulated ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Zhou et al. 2008 ) . 2.3 Why the 8-week disease-control endpoint Everything in an adaptive design lives or dies with how fast the outcome arrives. BATTLE chose disease control at 8 weeks (DCR@8w) — complete response, partial response, or stable disease by RECIST at week 8 — as the primary endpoint ( Kim et al. 2011 ) . The choice had empirical support: a Southwest Oncology Group analysis published while BATTLE was in development showed that disease control at 8 weeks predicted clinical benefit (survival) in advanced NSCLC ( Lara, Redman, and Kelly 2008 ) . It also had pragmatic virtues that a biostatistician should appreciate: it is quickly and objectively assessable, it suits the cytostatic profile of targeted agents (where tumor shrinkage is rare but stabilization is meaningful), and it turns around fast enough to inform randomization of the next patient ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Zhou et al. 2008 ) . The design paper was explicit that this short-turnaround property is what makes outcome-adaptive randomization viable at all ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) . 3 The BATTLE program at a glance Fact box — what is documented about BATTLE-1 BATTLE-1 was a randomized phase II, single-center (MD Anderson Cancer Center), open-label umbrella trial with four parallel phase II sub-studies, activated on November 30, 2006 and completed accrual on October 28, 2009 . It enrolled 341 patients, of whom 255 were randomized (equal randomization for the first 97 , outcome-adaptive randomization for the remaining 158 ). The primary endpoint was 8-week disease control (DCR@8w) . Approval came from the MD Anderson IRB and the U.S. Department of Defense; an independent Data and Safety Monitoring Board (chaired by Donald A. Berry) monitored the trial. Funding came in part from DoD grant W81XWH-6-1-0303 and NCI Cancer Center Support Grant CA016672, with support also acknowledged from Merck Research Laboratories and Bayer HealthCare ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Sub-study registrations on ClinicalTrials.gov: umbrella protocol NCT00409968, erlotinib NCT00410059, vandetanib (ZD6474) NCT00410189, erlotinib + bexarotene NCT00411632, sorafenib NCT00411671 (all activated November 2006). First, patients who progressed could re-enter the trial with a new biopsy and be re-randomized — hence the 17 second and 1 third randomizations documented in the CONSORT diagram ( Kim et al. 2011 ) . Second, a front-line companion program, BATTLE-FL (NCT01263782), was later registered and completed with 64 participants, but this article focuses on BATTLE-1 and BATTLE-2, which carry the published methods lessons ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Why the umbrella-plus-sub-studies structure mattered Structurally, BATTLE-1 was “one protocol, four trials”: a single consent, a single screening biopsy, and a single randomization engine serving four parallel phase II sub-studies ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . For a biostatistician the important consequence is shared learning : every patient’s outcome updated one common model, so information flowed across sub-studies through the hierarchical prior — something four separately conducted single-arm trials cannot do. The trialists explicitly credited this “all patients under one roof” feature with improving patient comparability and efficiency relative to sequential single-arm studies ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . 4 Inside the design: objectives, biomarker engine, and the Bayesian machinery 4.1 What the trial promised to deliver BATTLE aimed both to evaluate targeted therapies and establish a platform for estimating treatment-specific disease control rates (DCRs) within biomarker groups. Under one protocol, posterior probabilities governed three decisions ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) : Success: Declare an arm × marker-group cell successful if \(\Pr(\gamma_{jk} > 0.30 \mid 	ext{data}) \ge 0.80\) ( Equation 8 ), relative to the historical 30% DCR ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Lara, Redman, and Kelly 2008 ) . Futility: After adaptive randomization began, suspend a cell if \(\Pr(\gamma_{jk} > 0.50 \mid 	ext{data}) \le 0.10\) ( Equation 7 ). Suspension was reversible ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Adaptive randomization: Assign patients among eligible, active treatments in proportion to the posterior mean DCR for their marker group ( Equation 5 ) ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) . Simulation calibrated these thresholds to limit the success rate to 20% under a 30% true DCR, while achieving at least 80% power at a 60% DCR and up to 95% at an 80% DCR ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . The deliberately liberal 20% type I error reflected the platform’s exploratory purpose: prioritizing potentially effective treatments for confirmation rather than prematurely discarding them ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Zhou et al. 2008 ) . 4.2 The two-stage architecture Show the R code boxes <- data.frame ( x = c ( 5 , 5 , 5 , 5 , 5 , 5 , 1.7 , 3.9 , 6.1 , 8.3 ), y = c ( 9.35 , 8.05 , 6.75 , 5.35 , 3.95 , 2.55 , 0.7 , 0.7 , 0.7 , 0.7 ), w = c ( 7.4 , 6.2 , 7.6 , 8.2 , 6.8 , 6.8 , 2.1 , 2.1 , 2.1 , 2.1 ), h = c ( 1.15 , 1.0 , 1.15 , 1.35 , 1.15 , 1.15 , 1.0 , 1.0 , 1.0 , 1.0 ), fill = c ( "#D9E8F5" , "#D9E8F5" , "#FDEBD0" , "#DFF2E4" , "#E8E0F0" , "#E8E0F0" , "#FBE3E0" , "#FBE3E0" , "#FBE3E0" , "#FBE3E0" ), size = c ( 2.85 , 2.85 , 2.75 , 2.75 , 2.85 , 2.85 , 2.35 , 2.35 , 2.35 , 2.35 ), label = c ( "Relapsed / refractory advanced NSCLC

Every enrolled patient underwent a mandatory fresh core-needle biopsy; eleven biomarkers were classified into five ranked marker groups; the first 97 randomized patients were allocated equally to the four arms (building the prior for the model), and the remaining 158 were randomized adaptively in proportion to posterior mean 8-week DCRs in their marker group, restricted to arms for which the patient was eligible. Diagram based on Kim et al. ( 2011 ) , Zhou et al. ( 2008 ) , and Liu and Lee ( 2015 ) . Figure 2 shows the flow. Two design choices deserve attention. First, the burn-in stage had a specific statistical job : equal randomization built the “prior probability of disease control for a given treatment in a given marker group” that the adaptive engine would consume afterwards ( Kim et al. 2011 ) . The plan called for at least 80 equally randomized patients, sufficient — the designers judged — for every marker-group cell to contain at least one completed treatment ( Kim et al. 2011 ) ; in the event, equal randomization covered 97 patients (~38% of randomized patients), a point the team later flagged as a lesson (Section 6.2) ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Second, eligibility restricted the adaptive engine : arms had treatment-specific eligibility criteria, and only 14% of enrolled patients were eligible for all four arms, so the randomization denominator Ω shrank patient by patient ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . 4.3 From 11 biomarkers to 5 marker groups The biomarker panel was fixed in 2005 and prespecified before activation ( Kim et al. 2011 ) . Tumors were tested for mutations of EGFR , KRAS , and BRAF ; copy number (FISH) of EGFR and the cyclin D1 gene ( CCND1 ); and protein expression (IHC) of VEGF, VEGFR-2, RXRα, RXRβ, RXRγ, and cyclin D1 — eleven markers in total ( Kim et al. 2011 ) . Because dichotomizing eleven markers yields \(2^{11} = 2{,}048\) possible profiles, the team collapsed them into five ranked marker groups , assigning each patient to the highest-ranked positive group (ranked by the strength of available 2005-era evidence), with a fifth group for patients negative for everything or with missing/incomplete data ( Liu and Lee 2015 ; Kim et al. 2011 ) : Table 3: The five ranked marker groups. Grouping and ranking are documented in ( Kim et al. 2011 ) (methods) and ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) (Table 1 description); the sequential “highest-ranked positive group wins” rule is explicit in both. Rank Marker group Constituent biomarkers (any one positive) 1 EGFR EGFR mutation; EGFR amplification / high polysomy; increased EGFR copy number 2 KRAS/BRAF KRAS mutation; BRAF mutation 3 VEGF/VEGFR-2 VEGF overexpression; VEGFR-2 overexpression 4 RXR/cyclin D1 RXRα, RXRβ, or RXRγ overexpression; cyclin D1 overexpression; CCND1 amplification 5 None / unknown No study biomarker positive, or biomarker data missing or incomplete Keep Table 3 in mind — the grouping itself became the trial’s most-cited self-criticism (Sections 7 and 8): strong single-marker effects (e.g., EGFR mutation for erlotinib) were diluted when bundled with weaker markers in the same class ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . 4.4 The Bayesian hierarchical probit model BATTLE’s outcome model is a hierarchical probit model — elegant, easy to Gibbs-sample, and pedagogically ideal because every piece has a trial-level meaning ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) . For patient \(i\) in arm \(j \in \{1,2,3,4\}\) and marker group \(k \in \{1,\dots,5\}\) , define \(y_{ijk} \in \{0,1\}\) as the 8-week disease-control indicator. Introduce a latent variable \(z_{ijk}\) : \[ y_{ijk} = \mathbf{1}\{z_{ijk} > 0\}, \qquad z_{ijk} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{jk},\, 1) 	ag{1}\] Here \(\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}\) is the indicator function, \(z_{ijk}\) is an unobserved “tolerance” that tips the patient into disease control when positive, and the variance is fixed at 1 for identifiability (the probit scale has no free scale parameter) ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) . The disease-control probability for the cell \((j,k)\) is then a smooth function of the cell mean \(\mu_{jk}\) : \[ \gamma_{jk} \;=\; \Pr(y_{ijk} = 1) \;=\; \Pr(z_{ijk} > 0) \;=\; \Phi(\mu_{jk}), 	ag{2}\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. Intuition: \(\mu_{jk}\) is just the probit transform of the cell’s DCR — e.g., a DCR of 0.46 corresponds to \(\mu \approx 0.10\) , and 0.58 to \(\mu \approx 0.20\) . The hierarchy enters through the prior on the cell means. Within an arm, the five marker-group means are exchangeable around an arm-level effect \(\phi_j\) ; the arm effects are themselves exchangeable around zero ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) : \[ \mu_{jk} \sim \mathcal{N}(\phi_j,\, \sigma^2) \quad (k = 1,\dots,5), \qquad \phi_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, 	au^2) \quad (j = 1,\dots,4) 	ag{3}\] with \(\sigma^2 = 	au^2 = 10^6\) as the default vague configuration ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) . Read Equation 3 as two dials of partial pooling : small \(\sigma^2\) makes the marker groups within an arm share information heavily (each group’s estimate is pulled toward the arm effect \(\phi_j\) ); small \(	au^2\) makes the arms share information with each other. BATTLE ran these dials essentially open (vague priors), so borrowing happened only where the data themselves were concordant — the model “learns how much to borrow” from the observed pattern of subgroup results ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; S. M. Berry et al. 2010 ) . Given the observed disease-control indicators, the posterior combines a probit likelihood with the normal priors: \[ p(\mu, \phi \mid 	ext{data}) \;\propto\; \prod_{j=1}^{4} \prod_{k=1}^{5} \prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}} \Phi(\mu_{jk})^{y_{ijk}} \left[1 - \Phi(\mu_{jk})ight]^{1 - y_{ijk}} \;	imes\; \prod_{j,k} \mathcal{N}(\mu_{jk} \mid \phi_j, \sigma^2) \;	imes\; \prod_{j} \mathcal{N}(\phi_j \mid 0, 	au^2) 	ag{4}\] The symbols in Equation 4 : \(n_{jk}\) is the number of patients randomized to arm \(j\) within marker group \(k\) ; \(\mu\) collects all twenty cell means and \(\phi\) the four arm effects. The trial team computed these posteriors by Gibbs sampling from the full conditionals — a workload that was heavy for 2006 but is trivial today, and that BATTLE-1 automated in R behind a web service (Section 6) ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Interpretation — why a probit rather than a logit? The probit link is not a substantive claim about biology; it is a computational convenience . With normal priors on \(\mu_{jk}\) , the full conditionals are (truncated) normals, so Gibbs sampling is exact and fast — no Metropolis–Hastings tuning in the middle of a live trial. A logistic model with the same hierarchy (used later for BATTLE-2, ( Lee, Gu, and Liu 2010 ) ) would deliver nearly identical inferences; the choice reflects 2006-era Bayesian computation practice, an excellent example of letting the computing environment shape — not distort — the statistics. Figure 3 makes the “borrowing strength” idea concrete with a small simulation. Eight marker-group-like subgroups (n = 8 each) are generated from a probit-scale hierarchy similar in spirit to Equation 3 (subgroup means centered at a DCR of 40%, subgroup SD 0.35 on the probit scale). Open circles: raw subgroup DCRs. Subgroups whose raw rate is extreme are pulled toward the arm average — this is the ‘borrowing strength’ that stabilized all 20 cells of BATTLE-1 with small \(n_{jk}\) . 4.5 The adaptive-randomization engine Once every one of the 20 cells (4 arms × 5 groups) contained at least one patient with a known outcome, randomization switched from equal to outcome-adaptive . For the next patient in marker group \(k\) , the probability of assignment to arm \(j\) was proportional to the posterior mean disease-control rate of that cell, with two safeguards ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) : \[ w_{jk} \;=\;  rac{\hat\gamma_{jk}}{\sum_{\omega \in \Omega}\hat\gamma_{\omega k}}, \qquad \hat\gamma_{jk} = \max\! ig\{\, \mathbb{E}[\gamma_{jk} \mid 	ext{data}],\; 0.10 \, ig\} 	ag{5}\] In Equation 5 , \(\hat\gamma_{jk}\) is the posterior mean DCR for arm \(j\) in group \(k\) (floored at 0.10 so no non-suspended arm ever becomes essentially unreachable — the trial’s explicit minimum-allocation device ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) ), and \(\Omega\) is the set of arms that are both non-suspended for futility and eligible for that patient (recall: only 14% of patients were eligible for all four arms ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) ). The published worked example ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) makes the weights tangible: if the current posterior mean DCRs in a marker group were 0.6, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1, the assignment probabilities become 0.50, 0.25, 0.17, and 0.08. Two remarks for the practicing statistician. First, this is covariate-adjusted adaptive randomization : the weights are computed within marker group , so the adaptation respects the stratification — the trial learns “which arm works best for tumors like this one ” rather than a single global winner. Second, BATTLE-1’s rule is the plainest member of the broader family of Bayesian adaptive-randomization rules popularized by Thall and Wathen, who add a power smoothing so that early, noisy estimates do not over-steer allocation ( Thall and Wathen 2007 ) : \[ w_j^{(m)} \;=\;  rac{ ar p_j^{\,q(m)}}{\sum_{\ell}  ar p_\ell^{\,q(m)}}, \qquad q(m) \;=\;  rac{m/4 + 8}{m}, 	ag{6}\] where \(m\) indexes trial progress, \( ar p_j\) is the current probability that arm \(j\) is (or performs) best, and \(q(m) > 1\) early (dampening) falls below 1 later (sharpening). BATTLE-1 used the unsmoothed proportional form of Equation 5 ; its successor BATTLE-2 instead bounded the randomization probabilities (0.2–0.8 in stage 1, 0.1–0.9 in stage 2) to prevent extreme allocations from either noise or premature certainty ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . If you implement one of these designs today, the choice among {no smoothing, power smoothing, probability bounds} is exactly the kind of decision to justify by simulation. Figure 4 shows what the BATTLE-1-style engine does in silico when seeded with the trial’s own marginal response rates. A Beta–Bernoulli approximation of Equation 5 (not the trial’s probit model) allocates 244 sequential patients among four arms with true 8-week DCRs set to BATTLE’s observed marginal rates (erlotinib 34%, vandetanib 33%, erlotinib + bexarotene 50%, sorafenib 58%; Kim et al. ( 2011 ) ). Each point is the assignment probability at that patient; the 10% floor of Equation 5 and normalization over arms are applied. Weights drift toward the better arms as evidence accumulates; note they start near 0.25 (equal) and remain noisy because only the assigned arm’s outcome updates. In the real trial, additionally, 8-week outcomes arrive with delay, so the engine ran on partially stale data. 4.6 Futility monitoring: suspension, not execution After adaptive randomization began, each new outcome re-triggered a futility check for every cell. A cell was suspended — patients in marker group \(k\) could no longer be randomized to arm \(j\) — whenever \[ \Pr\{\gamma_{jk} > 0.50 \mid 	ext{data}\} \;\le\; 0.10, 	ag{7}\] i.e., when the data made it unlikely (posterior probability ≤ 10%) that the cell’s true DCR exceeded the 50% target ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Three features of this rule reward attention. It is cell-specific : the same arm could stay open for one marker group while suspended for another — the entire point of a biomarker-guided design. It is reversible : if later data (e.g., from other marker groups borrowed through the hierarchy) lifted the posterior back above the boundary, the cell reopened ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) . And there is no early stopping for efficacy : success was only declared at trial end, so adaptation and inference could never race each other ( Zhou et al. 2008 ) . The success rule itself, applied to every cell at the trial’s close, was \[ \Pr\{\gamma_{jk} > 0.30 \mid 	ext{data}\} \;\ge\; 0.80, 	ag{8}\] i.e., a posterior probability of at least 0.80 that the cell’s true DCR exceeds the 30% historical benchmark ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Kim et al. 2011 ) . An integrated web application tracked patients from registration and biopsy through biomarker classification, randomization, 8-week assessment, and follow-up. Data were stored in MD Anderson’s CORe environment and a study-specific SQL Server database ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . R code, invoked through web services, automatically updated posterior DCRs, randomization probabilities, and futility decisions whenever an outcome was recorded ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . This infrastructure illustrates the practical costs of adaptive trials: timely data entry, quality control, computation, and specialized software ( Lee and Chu 2012 ) . Endpoint timeliness was critical. Automated reminders prompted coordinators to schedule week-8 scans and escalated outcomes overdue by more than two weeks ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . A multidisciplinary endpoint committee, blinded to treatment assignment, adjudicated RECIST outcomes before they entered the randomization algorithm ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . ::: {.callout-tip appearance=“simple”} ## Why blinded adjudication mattered Each 8-week outcome influenced allocations for future patients. Knowledge of treatment could bias assessments, particularly stable-disease classifications, and propagate that bias through the adaptive algorithm. Blinded adjudication is therefore an important safeguard in outcome-adaptive trials ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . ::: ## Implementation lessons BATTLE required close coordination among clinicians, radiologists, pathologists, pharmacists, nurses, programmers, coordinators, and statisticians ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Its retrospective evaluation identified five main lessons ( Liu and Lee 2015 ; Kim et al. 2011 ) : Marker grouping diluted signals. Combining EGFR mutations with copy-number changes weakened predictive performance, while several prespecified markers were uninformative. Marker groupings should remain flexible when prior evidence is limited. Burn-in delayed adaptation. Requiring observations in every cell postponed adaptive randomization until approximately 40% of patients had enrolled. The investigators later recommended adapting after about 20–25%. Eligibility restricted adaptation. Only 14% of patients were eligible for all four treatments, so most allocations occurred within restricted arm sets \(\Omega\) ( Equation 5 ). Population drift changed eligibility. Increasing proportions of smokers and patients previously treated with erlotinib altered the available treatment sets. Adaptive trials should monitor such drift and consider covariate adjustment. Adaptation depends on biological separation. Outcome-adaptive randomization offers limited gains when treatments or biomarkers do not meaningfully discriminate outcomes ( Liu and Lee 2015 ; Lee, Chen, and Yin 2012 ) . ::: {.callout-note appearance=“simple”} ## BATTLE-2: redesigning around the lessons BATTLE-2 introduced adaptive randomization from the first patient, bounded allocation probabilities, and no prespecified marker groups. Candidate biomarkers were screened before the trial and evaluated through a Bayesian two-stage Lasso strategy. The design also added a stage-1 Go/No-Go decision, futility monitoring from patient 71, and a target of 400 evaluable patients, with at least 80% power and a 10% type I error rate. Show the R code tt <- seq ( 0 , 24 , by = 0.05 ) surv_df <- data.frame ( t = rep (tt, 2 ), S = c ( 0.5 ^ (tt / 1.9 ), 0.5 ^ (tt / 8.8 )), curve = rep ( c ( "PFS (median 1.9 months)" , "OS (median 8.8 months)" ), each = length (tt))) ggplot (surv_df, aes (t, 100 * S, colour = curve)) + geom_line ( linewidth = 0.9 ) + geom_vline ( xintercept = 8 , linetype = 2 , colour = "grey45" ) + geom_hline ( yintercept = 50 , linetype = 3 , colour = "grey60" ) + scale_colour_manual ( values = c (pal[ 1 ], pal[ 4 ])) + scale_y_continuous ( labels = percent) + labs ( x = "Months since randomization" , y = "Event-free proportion" , title = "Illustrative exponential reconstruction of the published medians" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = 8 , y = 93 , size = 2.9 , colour = "grey35" , label = "week 8: the primary endpoint's clock" ) Figure 12: Illustrative reconstruction — exponential survival curves calibrated to the published median PFS (1.9 months) and OS (8.8 months) for the overall randomized population ( Kim et al. 2011 ) . Under an exponential model with median m, S(t) = 0.5^(t/m) ( Equation 10 ). These are NOT Kaplan–Meier estimates from patient-level data — real curves bend and cross subgroups differently — but they give an honest visual sense of the temporal scale on which the 8-week endpoint sits: by the time the median patient had died, nearly a year had passed; by week 8 (dashed), most patients were still progression-free. \[ S(t) = 0.5^{\,t / m} 	ag{10}\] In Equation 10 , \(S(t)\) is the event-free proportion at time \(t\) and \(m\) the median event time in months; the exponential is the unique survival model in which the hazard is constant, and it is used here purely as a visual calibration device, not as an inferential claim. 8 Regulatory interactions, guidance, and the path to acceptance Because adaptive and biomarker-guided designs live or die by regulatory acceptance, this section addresses the question directly and in two layers: what is documented about BATTLE’s own regulatory interactions, and how the surrounding regulatory framework evolved around trials like it. Where we move from record to interpretation, we say so. 8.1 What is actually documented about BATTLE and regulators Fact box — documented regulatory touchpoints of the BATTLE program Oversight of BATTLE-1 was conventional and documented: approval by the MD Anderson IRB and the U.S. Department of Defense, monitoring by an independent DSMB (chaired by Donald A. Berry), and standard IND-era handling of the investigational agents ( Kim et al. 2011 ) . Agent status mattered. Two of the four agents were FDA-approved at the time (erlotinib, Nov 2004 ( Cohen, Johnson, and Pazdur 2005 ) ; sorafenib, Dec 2005, for renal-cell carcinoma ( Kane, Farrell, and Sabharwal 2006 ) ); vandetanib was not approved anywhere until April 2011 ( 2011 ) ; the erlotinib + bexarotene combination was investigational ( Kim et al. 2011 ) . BATTLE-1 was thus an investigator-initiated phase II platform, not a registration program. The documented FDA interaction belongs to BATTLE-2 : “Due to its exploratory nature, BATTLE-2 has received the investigational device exemption (IDE) waiver after a meeting with the FDA in January 2013” ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . The trial’s biopsy-and-biomarker workflow is what brings it into IDE territory, and the sponsor sought and documented FDA input on the adaptive design before opening stage 1 (trial registration NCT01248247; opened June 2011 at MD Anderson and Yale). Industry engaged publicly : the primary BATTLE-1 paper drew a companion commentary from scientists at Merck Research Laboratories framing the trial as “a bold step toward improving the efficiency of biomarker-based drug development” and highlighting simultaneous therapeutics–diagnostics development ( Rubin, Anderson, and Gause 2011 ) ; Merck scientists (D. Mauro, E. Rubin) later co-authored the BATTLE-2 primary paper ( Papadimitrakopoulou et al. 2016 ) . To our knowledge, no public record documents a special FDA review of BATTLE-1’s adaptive features of the kind later formalized in FDA’s adaptive-design guidance processes — consistent with its role as an exploratory, single-center, non-registration platform. (This is a statement about the absence of public documentation, not about private interactions.) 8.2 Interpretation: what BATTLE did and did not change for regulators Interpretation (clearly not a documented causal claim) BATTLE was never a registration trial, and it left no documented regulatory decision trail of its own. Its regulatory significance is better understood as feasibility testimony and methodological exemplar : it demonstrated to sponsors and reviewers alike that biopsy-mandated, biomarker-stratified, adaptively randomized platforms can be executed and monitored, and its statistical grammar — hierarchical models, posterior decision thresholds, simulated operating characteristics, prespecified adaptation rules — is precisely the grammar the 2019 FDA guidance later asks sponsors to speak ( 2019a ; Liu and Lee 2015 ; Lee and Chu 2012 ) . Three specific contrasts between BATTLE-style exploration and registration expectations are worth teaching: Error budgets. A deliberate 20% per-cell type I error rate is defensible for discovery platforms; regulators evaluating confirmatory claims ask for controlled family-wise (or at least clearly bounded) error across the adaptation and subgroup structure — the EMA paper and FDA final guidance both make this central ( 2007 , 2019a ) . Endpoint. An 8-week DCR enabled the adaptation but would not, by itself, support a therapeutic claim; registration examples of biomarker-guided approval (e.g., the erlotinib–cobas EGFR co-approval) rested on survival-benefit endpoints with validated diagnostics ( 2013 ; Cohen, Johnson, and Pazdur 2005 ) . Device–drug coupling. BATTLE used biomarkers for allocation learning , not for device-regulated patient selection claims ; the regulatory machinery for the latter (co-development, CDx PMA) is what later made biomarker-guided labels routine ( 2014 , 2019b ) . In our reading, BATTLE’s most durable regulatory contribution is cultural: along with I-SPY 2 ( Barker et al. 2009 ) , it normalized the idea that a trial’s decision engine can learn while protecting patients — and the eventual ICH E20 draft is, in effect, the codification of lessons from this generation of platform trials ( 2025 ; D. A. Berry 2012 ) . 9 Legacy: BATTLE-2 and the platform-trial era 9.1 BATTLE-2: the redesign, honestly reported BATTLE-2 (NCT01248247) redesigned the platform around every lesson of BATTLE-1: adaptive randomization from the first patient , stratified by KRAS status with probabilities bounded at 0.2–0.8 (stage 1) and 0.1–0.9 (stage 2); no prespecified marker grouping (>100 candidate markers screened pre-trial, refined in-trial via training–testing–validation and a Bayesian two-step Lasso); a Go/No-Go gate after stage 1; futility monitoring from patient 71; 450 planned enrollments (400 evaluable); and a documented FDA meeting (January 2013) with IDE waiver ( Liu and Lee 2015 ; Lee, Gu, and Liu 2010 ; Gu et al. 2016 ; Gu, Yin, and Lee 2013 ) . The design and other feature of the trial will be discussed in other article. 9.2 The era BATTLE helped open Contemporaneous commentaries recognized the moment — “a new BATTLE in the evolving war on cancer” ( Sequist, Muzikansky, and Engelman 2011 ) , and, from Merck, “a bold step toward improving the efficiency of biomarker-based drug development” ( Rubin, Anderson, and Gause 2011 ) . The direct descendants are familiar. I-SPY 2 embedded biomarker-adaptive randomization with Bayesian “graduation” rules in breast cancer ( Barker et al. 2009 ) . NCI-MATCH and Lung-MAP made molecular screening plus biomarker-matched assignment national infrastructure ( 2024b , 2024a ) . Reviewers of adaptive oncology cite BATTLE as the completed proof-of-concept for Bayesian adaptive, biomarker-guided randomization ( D. A. Berry 2012 ; Lee and Chu 2012 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . And the specific design ideas — hierarchical borrowing across subgroups, posterior-probability decision rules, allocation floors and bounds, burn-in stages — are now standard vocabulary in trial-design software and ICH E20 discussions ( 2025 ; S. M. Berry et al. 2010 ) . 10 Ten lessons for designing and analyzing biomarker-guided adaptive trials Operations are the design. The binding constraint on BATTLE was never computation; it was biopsy adequacy (82.9%), assay turnaround (2 weeks), and endpoint timeliness. Before promising any adaptation, measure — and prespecify minimum acceptable values for — the operational chain that feeds it ( Tam et al. 2013 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Pick an endpoint that outruns accrual. Adaptive randomization only helps if outcomes arrive faster than patients. The 8-week DCR was chosen for exactly this property and had survival-prediction evidence behind it ( Lara, Redman, and Kelly 2008 ; Zhou et al. 2008 ) . Budget the burn-in, don’t let it happen to you. Equal randomization builds the prior, but a “wait until every cell is filled” rule handed the calendar to the sparsest subgroup (~40% of the trial ran equally). A fixed proportion (20–25%) or model-based readiness criteria are safer ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Don’t bundle biomarkers you mean to learn about. Grouping preserved degrees of freedom but diluted EGFR -mutation signal and wasted the trial’s sparsest groups on uninformative RXR markers. Group only when prior evidence is genuinely symmetric across constituents; otherwise model individual markers ( Kim et al. 2011 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Keep allocation floors/bounds — and justify them by simulation. The 10% floor kept every open arm learnable; BATTLE-2’s 0.2–0.8 and 0.1–0.9 bounds prevent both starvation and premature commitment. Show that operating characteristics survive perturbing these constants ( ?@fig-sensitivity ) ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Simulate the eligibility structure, not just the biology. Only 14% of patients were eligible for all four arms; the effective randomization space is the intersection of futility, eligibility, and marker group. Your simulations should mimic that intersection ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . State decision thresholds and their error trade-off in advance. Null 30% / target 50% / success at 80% posterior / futility at 10% posterior — all prespecified, all calibrated by simulation, with the 20% type I error rate defended openly as a screening choice ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Kim et al. 2011 ) . Make futility reversible and adjudicate endpoints blinded. Cell-level suspension that can reopen, plus an endpoint review committee blinded to assignment, protects the integrity of the feedback loop into randomization ( Zhou et al. 2008 ; Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Watch for drift and say what adaptation does to comparisons. Monitor enrollment mix prospectively (BATTLE’s smokers/prior-erlotinib drift); plan covariate adjustment for between-arm contrasts, because adaptive allocation entangles arm with calendar time ( Liu and Lee 2015 ) . Separate the engine from the verdict. BATTLE’s adaptive machinery learned which cells were promising; it did not — and was never designed to — establish comparative efficacy. Design the confirmation path (randomized comparison, validated diagnostic, appropriate error budget) as part of the platform, not afterthought ( Kim et al. 2011 ; 2007 , 2019a ) . An Introduction to Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) Author Akif Mustafa ✉ Published June 1, 2026 1 Introduction The Cox proportional hazards (CPH) model is the go-to model for survival analysis. It is popular for good reasons: It is semi-parametric — no distributional assumption needed. It handles multiple predictor variables. It gives an easy-to-interpret summary: the hazard ratio (HR) . It handles censoring naturally. But it makes one strong assumption: proportional hazards (PH) . This means the hazard of the event in two groups must always remain proportional throughout the study period. Everything works well when this holds. What if it does not hold? When hazards are not proportional — for example, when survival curves cross, when there is a delayed treatment effect, or when the benefit diminishes over time — a single HR becomes misleading. It no longer summarizes the treatment effect well. Potential hazard scenarious In these situations, there are several analytical alternatives to the standard Cox model: Piecewise Cox model Cox model with time-varying coefficients Royston-Parmar parametric model Accelerated failure time (AFT) model Cure models Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) is one such alternative. It is practical, interpretable, and widely used when the proportional hazards assumption is violated. 2 What is RMST? The Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) up to a time point \(	au\) is: The average time a person survives from time 0 to time \(	au\) . Equivalently, the area under the survival curve \(S(t)\) from 0 to \(	au\) . Mathematically: \[ 	ext{RMST}(	au) = E[\min(T, 	au)] = \int_0^{	au} S(t)\, dt \] Two key points: “Restricted” means we only look up to a pre-specified horizon \(	au\) (e.g., 5 years), not to infinity. It is a non-parametric summary of the whole survival curve up to \(	au\) . No proportional hazards assumption. No specific model required. 2.1 Visualizing RMST: Area Under the Curve Code set.seed ( 1 ) tau <- 48 t_seq <- seq ( 0 , 60 , by = 0.1 ) s_t <- exp ( - 0.03 * t_seq) df_line <- data.frame ( time = t_seq, surv = s_t) df_shade <- data.frame ( time = c ( 0 , t_seq[t_seq <= tau], tau), surv = c ( 0 , s_t[t_seq <= tau], 0 ) ) ggplot () + geom_polygon ( data = df_shade, aes (time, surv), fill = "steelblue" , alpha = 0.35 ) + geom_line ( data = df_line, aes (time, surv), color = "steelblue" , linewidth = 1.2 ) + geom_vline ( xintercept = tau, linetype = "dashed" , color = "black" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau + 1.5 , y = 0.85 , label = expression (tau), size = 5 , hjust = 0 ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau / 2.5 , y = 0.22 , label = "RMST = Area 
 under S(t) 
 up to τ" , size = 3.8 , color = "steelblue4" , fontface = "bold" ) + labs ( title = "Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST)" , subtitle = paste0 ( "Shaded area = RMST up to τ = " , tau, " months" ), x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability S(t)" ) + scale_x_continuous ( breaks = seq ( 0 , 60 , 12 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) RMST is the area under the survival curve S(t) from time 0 to τ 2.2 RMST for Two Groups For two groups (e.g., treatment vs. control), the difference in RMST is the area between the two survival curves from 0 to \(	au\) . It tells you: on average, how much extra survival time does the treatment provide up to time \(	au\) ? Code set.seed ( 2 ) tau <- 48 t_seq <- seq ( 0 , 60 , by = 0.1 ) s_trt <- exp ( - 0.020 * t_seq) s_ctrl <- exp ( - 0.035 * t_seq) df_two <- data.frame ( time = t_seq, Treated = s_trt, Control = s_ctrl ) |> tidyr :: pivot_longer ( - time, names_to = "Group" , values_to = "Survival" ) df_between <- data.frame ( time = c (t_seq[t_seq <= tau], rev (t_seq[t_seq <= tau])), surv = c (s_trt[t_seq <= tau], rev (s_ctrl[t_seq <= tau])) ) ggplot () + geom_polygon ( data = df_between, aes (time, surv), fill = "gold" , alpha = 0.5 ) + geom_line ( data = df_two, aes (time, Survival, color = Group), linewidth = 1.2 ) + geom_vline ( xintercept = tau, linetype = "dashed" , color = "black" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau + 1.5 , y = 0.9 , label = expression (tau), size = 5 , hjust = 0 ) + annotate ( "text" , x = 15 , y = 0.55 , label = "RMST 
 Difference" , size = 3.8 , color = "darkgoldenrod" , fontface = "bold" ) + scale_color_manual ( values = c ( "Control" = "tomato" , "Treated" = "steelblue" )) + labs ( title = "RMST Difference Between Two Groups" , subtitle = "Shaded area = difference in RMST up to τ" , x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability S(t)" ) + scale_x_continuous ( breaks = seq ( 0 , 60 , 12 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) + theme ( legend.position = "bottom" ) RMST difference = shaded area between the two survival curves up to τ 3 Why RMST? Limitations of the Cox Model The Cox model gives hazard ratios. HRs are useful, but they have real limitations. 3.1 PH Assumption The Cox model requires proportional hazards . If hazards are not proportional (crossing curves, delayed effects, diminishing benefits), a single HR is misleading. In immuno-oncology, for example, survival curves often separate late or cross altogether. The PH assumption frequently fails here. 3.2 HR is Relative, Not Absolute HR = 0.6 means a 40% lower hazard. But what does that mean in months of life gained ? That depends on the baseline hazard — a detail HR does not convey. Clinicians and patients often more interested in: “How much extra time do I get, on average?” than about a hazard ratio. 3.3 HR is Model-Based The Cox HR is a model-based summary. If the model is wrong — due to non-proportional hazards or misspecification — the HR can be biased and difficult to interpret. 3.4 How RMST Addresses These Limitations Issue Cox HR RMST Requires PH assumption ✅ Yes ❌ No Absolute effect size ❌ No ✅ Yes (time gained) Model-free ❌ No ✅ Yes (from KM curve) Easy clinical communication ⚠️ Moderate ✅ High RMST is not a replacement for the Cox model in all settings. It is a complement and an alternative — especially when PH fails or an absolute effect size matters more. 4 When to Use RMST? 4.1 Use RMST When: 1. Non-proportional hazards (NPH) are present Crossing survival curves Delayed treatment effect (early overlap, later separation) Diminishing benefit (early benefit that later fades) 2. An absolute effect is more meaningful than a relative one “Patients in the active arm survive on average 3 months longer over 5 years.” Health economics: quantifying life-years gained within a fixed horizon. 3. You want a model-free summary No reliance on a correctly specified Cox model. Simple, robust comparison of two survival curves up to \(	au\) . 4. As a supplement to HRs and log-rank tests Even when PH holds, RMST can be reported alongside the HR to provide an absolute effect estimate. Many recent clinical trials in oncology report both HR and RMST difference. 4.2 You Probably Do Not Need RMST When: PH holds well, and HR is sufficient for your scientific or clinical question, and There is no strong demand for an absolute “time gained” interpretation. 5 Estimation 5.1 Single Group The steps are straightforward: Estimate the survival curve \(S(t)\) using the Kaplan–Meier estimator. Choose a clinically relevant truncation time \(	au\) (e.g., 5 years). Pre-specify this before the analysis. Compute the area under the KM curve from 0 to \(	au\) using the trapezoidal rule (sum of rectangles under the step function). Estimate the standard error using a Greenwood-type formula. Construct confidence intervals using asymptotic normality (for large samples). 5.2 Two-Group Comparison Let \(S_1(t)\) and \(S_0(t)\) be the KM curves in the treatment and control groups. \[ 	ext{RMST}_1(	au) = \int_0^{	au} S_1(t)\, dt \qquad 	ext{RMST}_0(	au) = \int_0^{	au} S_0(t)\, dt \] Three key summary measures: 1. Difference in RMST (most common) \[ \Delta(	au) = 	ext{RMST}_1(	au) - 	ext{RMST}_0(	au) = \int_0^{	au} [S_1(t) - S_0(t)]\, dt \] Interpretation : On average, how many extra months does treatment provide by time \(	au\) ? 2. Ratio of RMST \[  rac{	ext{RMST}_1(	au)}{	ext{RMST}_0(	au)} \] Interpretation : Relative increase in average survival time up to \(	au\) . 3. Ratio of Restricted Mean Time Lost (RMTL) \[ 	ext{RMTL}(	au) = 	au - 	ext{RMST}(	au) \] This is the average time lost due to the event before \(	au\) . \[ 	ext{RMTL ratio} =  rac{	ext{RMTL}_1(	au)}{	ext{RMTL}_0(	au)} \] Interpretation : Useful when the focus is on time lost rather than time lived. Inference (difference and ratio): Based on asymptotic normality with Greenwood-based variance estimates. Provides standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values. 6 Choosing \(	au\) The choice of \(	au\) matters. Some guidance: \(	au\) should be clinically chosen and pre-specified before the analysis (e.g., 5-year RMST in a cancer trial). It must fall within the observed follow-up where enough events have occurred and the KM estimate is reliable (i.e., do not extrapolate beyond the last event time). A common practical rule: set \(	au\) at or before the minimum of the two groups’ last event times , or at a clinically meaningful landmark such as 1, 2, or 5 years. Some methods choose \(	au\) adaptively, but a fixed, pre-specified \(	au\) is preferred for transparency and interpretability. Effect of τ choice on RMST estimation. The shaded areas show RMST for three different values of τ. 7 Example in R Here we simulate a delayed treatment effect: Before 12 months: treatment and control have similar hazard. After 12 months: treatment hazard becomes lower. This violates proportional hazards. 7.1 Simulate Data Code library (survival) library (survRM2) library (ggplot2) library (dplyr) library (tibble) library (knitr) library (kableExtra) set.seed ( 999 ) n <- 600 arm <- rbinom (n, 1 , 0.5 ) # 0 = control, 1 = treatment # Control: constant hazard throughout t_control <- rexp (n, rate = 0.05 ) # Treatment: same hazard before 12 months, lower hazard after 12 months t1 <- rexp (n, rate = 0.05 ) t_treat <- ifelse (t1 < 12 , t1, 12 + rexp (n, rate = 0.02 )) time_event <- ifelse (arm == 0 , t_control, t_treat) # Administrative censoring at 36 months time <- pmin (time_event, 36 ) status <- as.integer (time_event <= 36 ) dat <- tibble ( time = time, status = status, arm = factor (arm, levels = c ( 0 , 1 ), labels = c ( "Control" , "Treatment" )) ) # Summary table dat |> group_by (arm) |> summarise ( N = n (), Events = sum (status), Censored = N - Events, Max_followup = round ( max (time), 1 ), .groups = "drop" ) |> kable ( caption = "Summary of simulated dataset" , col.names = c ( "Group" , "N" , "Events" , "Censored" , "Max Follow-up (months)" ) ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) Summary of simulated dataset Group N Events Censored Max Follow-up (months) Control 302 248 54 36 Treatment 298 208 90 36 7.2 Kaplan–Meier Curves Code fit_km <- survfit ( Surv (time, status) ~ arm, data = dat) # Extract KM step data for ggplot km_df <- data.frame ( time = fit_km $ time, surv = fit_km $ surv, strata = rep ( names (fit_km $ strata), fit_km $ strata) ) |> mutate ( arm = sub ( "arm=" , "" , strata)) # Add time = 0 rows for each group time0 <- data.frame ( time = 0 , surv = 1 , strata = NA , arm = c ( "Control" , "Treatment" ) ) km_plot_df <- bind_rows (time0, km_df) |> arrange (arm, time) ggplot (km_plot_df, aes ( x = time, y = surv, color = arm)) + geom_step ( linewidth = 1 ) + scale_color_manual ( name = "Group" , values = c ( "Control" = "tomato" , "Treatment" = "steelblue" ) ) + scale_x_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 36 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 36 , 6 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + labs ( title = "Kaplan–Meier Curves: Delayed Treatment Effect" , subtitle = "Curves overlap early and diverge after ~12 months" , x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability" ) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) + theme ( legend.position = "bottom" ) Kaplan–Meier curves for simulated delayed treatment effect data The curves initially overlap, reflecting similar early hazards. After 12 months they diverge as the treatment arm benefits from a lower hazard. This pattern suggests a violation of the proportional hazards assumption. 7.3 Check the Proportional Hazards Assumption 7.3.1 First, lets fit the cox PH model Code cox_fit <- coxph ( Surv (time, status) ~ arm, data = dat) summary (cox_fit) Call: coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ arm, data = dat) n= 600, number of events= 456 coef exp(coef) se(coef) z Pr(>|z|) armTreatment -0.23982 0.78677 0.09429 -2.543 0.011 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95 armTreatment 0.7868 1.271 0.654 0.9465 Concordance= 0.518 (se = 0.013 ) Likelihood ratio test= 6.5 on 1 df, p=0.01 Wald test = 6.47 on 1 df, p=0.01 Score (logrank) test = 6.5 on 1 df, p=0.01 7.3.2 Now, check the PH assumption using schoenfeld test Code zph <- cox.zph (cox_fit) # Print test result as a neat table as.data.frame (zph $ table) |> kable ( caption = "Schoenfeld residuals test for proportional hazards" , digits = 4 ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) Schoenfeld residuals test for proportional hazards chisq df p arm 8.4937 1 0.0036 GLOBAL 8.4937 1 0.0036 A p-value below 0.05 on the Schoenfeld test indicates a violation of the PH assumption. 7.3.3 Plot the Schoenfeld residuals for visual inspection Code plot (zph, main = "Schoenfeld Residuals Over Time" ) abline ( h = 0 , lty = 2 , col = "grey50" ) Scaled Schoenfeld residuals. A flat line suggests PH holds; a trend suggests violation. A non-linear trend in the residuals plot confirms this. PH is violated here — making RMST a better choice. 7.4 Compute RMST We use the survRM2 package and set \(	au = 36\) months. Code tau_val <- 36 rm <- rmst2 ( time = dat $ time, status = dat $ status, arm = as.integer (dat $ arm == "Treatment" ), # 1 = treatment, 0 = control tau = tau_val ) rm The truncation time: tau = 36 was specified. Control) 1.89 -0.22 4.00 0.0789 RMST (arm=1)/(arm=0) RMST Ratio (Treatment / Control) 1.11 0.99 1.25 0.0780 RMTL (arm=1)/(arm=0) RMTL Ratio (Treatment / Control) 0.90 0.80 1.01 0.0816 7.5 Visualize RMST Code # Fit separate KM curves for each arm km_trt <- survfit ( Surv (time, status) ~ 1 , data = filter (dat, arm == "Treatment" )) km_ctrl <- survfit ( Surv (time, status) ~ 1 , data = filter (dat, arm == "Control" )) # Helper: convert survfit object to a step-function data frame km_to_df <- function (km_obj, group_label) { data.frame ( time = c ( 0 , km_obj $ time), surv = c ( 1 , km_obj $ surv), group = group_label ) } df_trt <- km_to_df (km_trt, "Treatment" ) df_ctrl <- km_to_df (km_ctrl, "Control" ) # Helper: build a closed polygon for shading up to tau make_shade <- function (df, tau_limit) { # Keep only time points up to tau df_trunc <- df[df $ time <= tau_limit, ] # Add a closing point at tau with the last survival value df_trunc <- rbind (df_trunc, data.frame ( time = tau_limit, surv = tail (df_trunc $ surv, 1 ), group = df_trunc $ group[ 1 ])) # Close the polygon back to zero data.frame ( time = c ( 0 , df_trunc $ time, tau_limit, 0 ), surv = c ( 0 , df_trunc $ surv, 0 , 0 ), group = df_trunc $ group[ 1 ] ) } shade_trt <- make_shade (df_trt, tau_val) shade_ctrl <- make_shade (df_ctrl, tau_val) ggplot () + # Shaded RMST areas geom_polygon ( data = shade_trt, aes (time, surv), fill = "steelblue" , alpha = 0.25 ) + geom_polygon ( data = shade_ctrl, aes (time, surv), fill = "tomato" , alpha = 0.25 ) + # KM step curves geom_step ( data = df_trt, aes (time, surv, color = "Treatment" ), linewidth = 1 ) + geom_step ( data = df_ctrl, aes (time, surv, color = "Control" ), linewidth = 1 ) + # Tau line geom_vline ( xintercept = tau_val, linetype = "dashed" , color = "black" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau_val - title: Multi-Crossover Designs in RCTs
text: Multi-Crossover Designs in RCTs Code What you gain by adding periods — and what it costs Author Akif Mustafa ✉ Published September 11, 2026 Abstract A practical guide to multi-crossover (higher-order) randomized controlled trial designs: how they are structured, how they are analysed, what they buy you, and when they break. Table of contents Table of contents 1 Why add periods? 1.1 The standard crossover, briefly 2 Design configurations 2.1 Replicated (two-treatment) designs 2.2 Multi-treatment (Williams) designs 3 Planning a multi-crossover trial 4 Statistical considerations 4.1 Choose the estimand first 4.2 Where the variability lives 4.3 Biases to design against 4.4 Analysis methods 4.5 Handling carryover 5 What you gain 5.1 Precision, and therefore sample size 5.2 Confounding, and repeated self-control 5.3 Where the design fits 6 What it costs 6.1 Dropout and duration 6.2 Assumptions that must actually hold 6.3 Carryover survives washout more often than you’d like 6.4 Missing data gets complicated 6.5 Functional unblinding 7 Case studies 8 Summary 9 References 9.1 Trials and examples 9.2 Methodological In one paragraph. A standard crossover gives each participant two treatments in two periods. A multi-crossover design gives them three or more. That extra structure lets you estimate within-subject variability per treatment, estimate carryover instead of assuming it away, compare more than two treatments, and survive dropout. The price is a longer trial, heavier logistics, and a stricter set of assumptions. 1 Why add periods? In a parallel-group trial, each participant gets one treatment. Comparisons are made between people, so between-subject variability sits squarely in the denominator of your test statistic and inflates the sample size you need. A crossover design removes that. Each participant receives more than one treatment in a randomised order, so the comparison is made within a person. When treatment effects are fast, reversible, and repeatedly measurable, this can be dramatically more efficient. The familiar AB/BA crossover, however, is a fragile instrument. Carryover is aliased with the treatment-by-period interaction, so the two cannot be separated. A participant who drops out after the first period contributes nothing to the paired comparison. And only two treatments can be compared. Adding periods fixes much of this. That is the subject of this article. 1.1 The standard crossover, briefly Figure 1: Standard two-period, two-sequence (AB/BA) crossover. Four terms recur throughout: Period — an interval during which a participant receives and is assessed on one treatment. Sequence — the order of treatments assigned to a participant (AB, BA, ABAB, …). Washout — the gap between periods, long enough for the previous treatment’s effects to dissipate. Within-subject comparison — each participant’s response on one treatment compared against their own response on another. Table 1: What breaks in a two-period crossover, and how extra periods help. Limitation Two-Period Crossover Multi-Crossover Resolution Carryover aliased with treatment × period interaction Carryover can be tested, but only with very low power, and cannot be separated from treatment × period Extra periods break the aliasing; carryover is estimable in balanced designs Only two treatments comparable One pairwise comparison Williams and Latin Square designs handle ≥ 3 treatments Dropout after Period 1 destroys the pairing Participant contributes no within-subject information Completing ≥ 2 of ≥ 3 periods still yields within-subject comparisons No treatment-specific within-subject variance Only a pooled within-subject variance is estimable Replicated designs give a separate variance per treatment 2 Design configurations A multi-crossover (or higher-order) design is a crossover trial with three or more periods. It may involve two treatments repeated (a replicated crossover) or three or more treatments each given at least once (a multi-treatment crossover). Two closely related designs are worth naming because they appear constantly in practice: Latin Square crossover — number of periods equals number of treatments, each treatment appearing once per period across the sequence set. Williams design — a balanced Latin Square in which every treatment precedes and follows every other treatment equally often, giving balance for first-order carryover. 2.1 Replicated (two-treatment) designs Table 2: Common replicated crossover configurations for two treatments (T = test, R = reference). Design Sequences Periods What it estimates Full replicate (2×2×4) TRTR, RTRT 4 Within-subject variance for both T and R Full replicate, 4-sequence TRTR, RTRT, TRRT, RTTR 4 Within-subject variance for both T and R Partial replicate (2×3×3) TRR, RTR, RRT 3 Within-subject variance for R only Two-sequence, four-period TTRR, RRTT 4 Within-subject variance for both T and R Why replicate? Only a replicated design can estimate the within-subject variance separately for each treatment . That is exactly what reference-scaled average bioequivalence requires for highly variable drug products — which is why four-period and partial-replicate designs dominate the bioequivalence literature. 2.2 Multi-treatment (Williams) designs A Williams design is constructed so that each treatment appears equally often in each period, and each treatment is immediately preceded by every other treatment equally often. Table 3: Williams design for three treatments: six sequences, three periods. Sequence Period 1 Period 2 Period 3 Sequence 1 A B C Sequence 2 B C A Sequence 3 C A B Sequence 4 C B A Sequence 5 A C B Sequence 6 B A C For an even number of treatments t , a Williams design needs t sequences; for an odd t , it needs 2 t . So four treatments fit into a balanced 4×4 square: Table 4: Williams design for four treatments: four sequences, four periods. Sequence Period 1 Period 2 Period 3 Period 4 Sequence 1 A B C D Sequence 2 B D A C Sequence 3 C A D B Sequence 4 D C B A When the number of treatments makes full balance impractical, partially balanced designs achieve balance for a subset of comparisons — a workable compromise. A note on Balaam’s design Balaam’s design (sequences AA, AB, BA, BB) has only two periods, so it is not a multi-crossover design by the definition used here. It is included in discussions like this one because the same-treatment sequences let you estimate direct treatment and carryover effects — the same problem multi-period designs solve, tackled by adding sequences instead of periods. 3 Planning a multi-crossover trial Before analysis, five planning decisions determine whether the design will work. 1. Number of periods. Each additional period increases precision but also dropout, duration, and cost. Choose the smallest p that answers your question: 3 if you need carryover estimable or a third treatment; 4 if you need treatment-specific within-subject variances. 2. Washout duration. Set it from pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, not convenience. A common rule of thumb is 5–7 elimination half-lives, but calibrate to the longest-acting treatment and to pharmacodynamic recovery, which can outlast drug clearance. In a multi-crossover design the washout must be adequate at every transition. 3. Run-in and period-specific baselines. A run-in stabilises the condition and reduces regression to the mean when participants are enrolled on extreme values. Collecting a baseline before each period gives you a direct check that participants returned to their starting state — the single most useful empirical evidence that the washout worked. 4. Sample size. For a continuous outcome, two treatments, p periods with p /2 replicates each, total participants for power \(1-\beta\) at two-sided \(\alpha\) : \[N \;=\; \frac{4\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^{2}\,\sigma_w^{2}}{p\,\delta^{2}}\] which reduces to the familiar \(2(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})^2\sigma_w^2/\delta^2\) when p = 2. Inflate for anticipated dropout, and note that only \(\sigma_w^2\) appears — the between-subject variance has vanished. 5. Randomisation and simulation. Allocate with stratified permuted blocks whose block size is a multiple of the number of sequences, so period and sequence stay balanced. Because closed-form power formulae ignore dropout, carryover and unbalanced sequences, simulate the design under realistic scenarios before committing. 4 Statistical considerations 4.1 Choose the estimand first The repeated-measures structure supports several distinct quantities. Pre-specify which one you want, because it determines the model. Population-average effect — the mean difference averaged across the population. Targeted by marginal models (GEE). Relevant for treatment policy. Subject-specific effect — the difference for a given individual, or the distribution of individual effects. Targeted by mixed models. Relevant for individualised decisions. Beyond the mean effect you may care about heterogeneity of response (the treatment-by-subject interaction, which is what makes N-of-1 designs interesting) and consistency across periods (the treatment-by-period interaction, which detects tolerance, learning effects, or carryover contamination). 4.2 Where the variability lives Figure 2: Between- and within-subject variability across four periods. Crossover analysis removes the between-subject component from the treatment comparison; the extra periods let you estimate the within-subject component directly. Between-subject variance ( \(\sigma_b^2\) ) — differences in baseline level across participants. Dominates parallel-group trials; removed by within-subject differencing. Handled as a random subject effect. Within-subject variance ( \(\sigma_w^2\) ) — variation in one participant’s response to the same treatment on different occasions. This is what drives your sample size. In replicated designs it can be estimated per treatment. Period-to-period variation — temporal trends, seasonality, practice effects. Handled as a fixed period effect; biases the comparison only if the design is unbalanced. 4.3 Biases to design against Table 5: Systematic effects in multi-crossover trials, and how to handle them. Effect Threat to Validity Design-Stage Mitigation Analysis-Stage Mitigation Period effect Confounds the treatment comparison when the design is unbalanced Balanced designs (Williams, Latin Square) Fixed period effect Sequence effect May signal differential carryover or prognostic imbalance Randomisation with adequate sample size Fixed sequence effect Carryover effect Biases the treatment effect; the most serious threat in crossover trials Adequate washout; balanced designs Carryover-adjusted sensitivity analysis (@sec-carryover) Time trend Systematic drift unrelated to treatment Limit total duration; enrol stable disease Time covariate in the model Regression to the mean Inflates the apparent effect in the first period Run-in period; period-specific baselines Baseline adjustment 4.4 Analysis methods For a continuous outcome the linear mixed-effects model is the default: fixed effects for treatment, period and sequence, a random intercept for participant, and optionally a carryover term. It tolerates unbalanced data from dropout and yields both subject-specific and population-average estimates. Table 6: Analytical options and when each applies. Method Outcome Type Estimand Notes Linear mixed model (LMM) Continuous Subject-specific and population-average Default choice; handles missing data under MAR; assumes normal residuals Generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) Binary, count Subject-specific (conditional) Logit or log link; convergence can be fragile with small N Generalized estimating equations (GEE) Any (via link) Population-average (marginal) Needs adequate N for the sandwich estimator; no subject-specific estimates Bayesian hierarchical model Any Subject-specific, full posterior Best for small N, sparse data, and N-of-1 aggregation; prior sensitivity applies Repeated measures ANOVA Continuous Population-average within blocks Requires complete, balanced data and compound symmetry; largely superseded 4.5 Handling carryover Prevent it by design. An adequate washout, calibrated to pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, is the primary safeguard. If the washout is pharmacologically defensible, the no-carryover assumption is defensible too. Assess it by analysis. In a design with sufficient degrees of freedom — a four-period replicate or a Williams design — include first-order carryover as a fixed effect in a pre-specified sensitivity analysis. If the treatment estimate barely moves, you have empirical reassurance. If it moves a lot, re-examine the washout and qualify your conclusions. Do not use the old two-stage procedure. Grizzle’s (1965) approach — test for carryover, then analyse as a crossover if non-significant and as a first-period parallel trial if significant — was dismantled by Senn (1993, 2002) on four grounds: The preliminary test has very low power, so a non-significant result is not evidence of absence. Conditioning the analysis on the test inflates the overall Type I error rate. It fails precisely when it is needed: undetected carryover leaves you with a biased crossover analysis. Reverting to first-period data discards the within-subject information that motivated the design. Critical reminder Never fall back on a first-period-only analysis because carryover was “detected”. Use a design in which carryover can be estimated directly, and report the sensitivity analysis alongside the primary one. 5 What you gain 5.1 Precision, and therefore sample size Each additional period adds within-subject replication. For a two-treatment replicated design with p periods, the variance of the treatment effect is proportional to \(1/p\) , so relative to a two-period crossover it falls as \(2/p\) . Figure 3: Variance of the treatment effect estimate relative to a two-period crossover, for two-treatment replicated designs with an even number of periods (2/p). Odd-period designs are not on this curve. Against a parallel-group trial the gain is larger still, and it scales with the intraclass correlation. Using total participants and a common effect size \(\delta\) on the total-SD scale, the ratio of crossover to parallel sample size is \((1-\text{ICC})\cdot 2/p\) . Figure 4: Total sample size for a crossover design as a proportion of the parallel-group requirement, as a function of the ICC. Ratio = (1 − ICC) × 2/p, matching the sample size formula in Section 3. For ICC between 0.5 and 0.8 — common for pharmacokinetic endpoints, physiological measurements and symptom scores — a two-period crossover needs roughly 20–50% of the parallel-group sample size, and a four-period replicate roughly 10–25% . Figure 5: Total participants for 80% power to detect δ = 0.5 total-SD units (two-sided α = 0.05), assuming ICC = 0.7, no carryover, no dropout, equal variances and perfect balance. Derived from the same formula as the curves above. This is decisive in rare diseases, paediatric subgroups and narrow phenotypes , where a parallel trial simply cannot be powered. At the limit, N-of-1 designs use repeated crossover cycles within a single patient, and aggregating several N-of-1 trials recovers population-level estimates. 5.2 Confounding, and repeated self-control Because every participant receives every treatment, there is no baseline imbalance to worry about: confounding by any stable participant-level characteristic — measured or not — is eliminated by construction. This does not extend to time-varying confounders, carryover, or differential dropout, all of which remain live threats. Repetition adds two things beyond the group mean: individual-level treatment effects , and the reproducibility of those effects across occasions, which distinguishes consistent responders from noisy ones. Figure 6: Within-subject comparisons in a four-period replicated crossover (ABAB). Each participant contributes multiple paired A-vs-B contrasts. 5.3 Where the design fits Table 7: Suitability by treatment onset and offset characteristics. Treatment Characteristic Examples Suitability Rapid onset and offset (hours to days) Bronchodilators, acute analgesics, PK studies Excellent — short periods allow many cycles Moderate onset and offset (days to weeks) Antihypertensives, antihistamines, migraine prophylaxis Good — feasible period and washout durations Slow onset, prolonged effect (weeks to months) Antidepressants, immunomodulators Limited — long washouts stretch the trial badly Permanent or disease-modifying effect Vaccines, gene therapies, surgical interventions Not suitable — reversibility assumption fails 6 What it costs 6.1 Dropout and duration Every extra period means more visits, more assessments and more elapsed time, so withdrawal accumulates. Figure 7: Retention under a constant 8% per-period dropout, for designs of 2, 4 and 6 periods. Multi-crossover designs lose more participants in absolute terms, but a partial completer still contributes within-subject information. Worse, if dropout is differential — participants leaving preferentially during a poorly tolerated treatment — the missing-at-random assumption behind your primary analysis fails. Total participant time is: \[T_{\text{total}} = T_{\text{screen}} + T_{\text{run-in}} + p \cdot T_{\text{treatment}} + (p - 1) \cdot T_{\text{washout}}\] Table 8: Total duration for representative configurations (screening 2 weeks, run-in 2 weeks). Design Periods Treatment (weeks) Washout (weeks) Total (weeks) Total (months) 2-period (standard crossover) 2 4 2 14 3.2 3-period (Williams, 3 treatments) 3 4 2 20 4.6 4-period (replicated crossover) 4 4 2 26 6.0 4-period (short treatment periods) 4 2 1 15 3.5 6-period (N-of-1, 3 pairs) 6 2 1 21 4.8 Long per-participant timelines also carry an opportunity cost: delayed evidence, delayed regulatory decisions. 6.2 Assumptions that must actually hold Figure 8: Core assumptions and the consequence of violating each. Table 9: Settings where a crossover design should not be used. Clinical Setting Assumption Violated Reason Oncology (curative chemotherapy) Reversibility; disease modification Disease state is irreversibly altered Vaccine trials Reversibility (immune memory) Immune response persists; no washout is possible Surgical interventions Reversibility (structural change) Anatomical changes are permanent Gene therapy Reversibility (permanent modification) Irreversible by design Acute infections Stable disease (self-limiting) Condition resolves spontaneously Rapidly progressive neurodegeneration Stable disease (progressive) Progression between periods confounds the comparison 6.3 Carryover survives washout more often than you’d like Figure 9: First- and higher-order carryover in a four-period design. Balanced designs protect against first-order carryover, not higher-order. Three mechanisms defeat a nominally adequate washout: Pharmacodynamic persistence — enzyme induction or receptor downregulation outlasts drug clearance. Psychological carryover — the experience of one treatment colours how symptoms are perceived and reported on the next. No washout removes this. Higher-order carryover — residual effects from two or more periods back. Balanced designs distribute first-order carryover evenly; they offer no equivalent protection here. 6.4 Missing data gets complicated Figure 10: Missing data patterns in a four-period design: monotone dropout versus intermittent non-response. Pre-specify a primary analysis under MAR using mixed models, plus sensitivity analyses under MNAR — pattern-mixture models, tipping-point analyses, or controlled imputation — and a rule for handling partial period data and intercurrent events under the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework. 6.5 Functional unblinding Crossover participants can compare their own experiences across periods, which a parallel-group participant cannot. Distinct side-effect profiles, formulation differences, or a large efficacy gap can all reveal treatment identity, and the risk rises with each additional period. Mitigations — active placebo, matched formulations, double-dummy administration, objective co-primary endpoints, and a post-study blinding index (James or Bang) — reduce the problem without eliminating it. Build them in at the design stage. 7 Case studies Registry identifiers, sample sizes and design descriptions below should be re-verified against the primary sources before publication. Replicated designs Partial replicate (3-period, 2-treatment) Williams designs Three treatments, three periods Balaam’s design Replicated crossovers dominate bioequivalence work, where the goal is to estimate intra-subject variability for reference-scaled assessment of highly variable drugs. Figure 11: Full-replicate crossover (TRTR/RTRT): each formulation is given twice. Table 10: Examples of replicated crossover designs. Trial Registry Design Key Feature Albendazole bioequivalence NCT06201559 4-period, 2-sequence full replicate (TRTR / RTRT) Test and reference 400 mg tablets each given twice per participant, enabling intra-subject variability estimation for both formulations Desmopressin nasal spray bioequivalence PMID 14564429 4-period, 2-sequence replicate High PK variability of intranasal peptides would have made a 2-period design impractically large; each formulation given twice with ≥ 1-week washout An intermediate between the standard crossover and the full replicate: the reference is given twice, the test once, so reference within-subject variability is estimable with one fewer period. Figure 12: Partially replicated three-period design (TRR / RTR / RRT). Captopril bioequivalence (NCT04878315) used exactly this FDA-recommended structure, giving the reference twice to support reference-scaled assessment while sparing participants a fourth period. Ibandronic acid bioequivalence ( Drugs in R&D , 2014) used the same three-way, reference-replicated family with a 14-day washout, single-dose, open-label, fasting. Used when three or more treatments need simultaneous within-subject comparison with first-order carryover balance. Table 11: Examples of Williams design trials. Trial Reference Design Treatments Key Feature Naloxone PK evaluation NCT05363501 4-period, 4-sequence Williams design Naloxone nasal swab, nasal spray, intramuscular injection Registered explicitly as a balanced 4-way Williams crossover; each formulation preceded and followed every other equally often Centanafadine thorough QT study Published (Otsuka / Supernus) 3-period, 6-sequence Williams square Centanafadine, placebo, moxifloxacin (positive control) Double-blind, full-block Williams square in 30 healthy adults, randomisation stratified by sex Table 12: Three-period, three-treatment crossover trials. Trial Reference Treatments Key Feature PT007 asthma study NCT06644924 AS MDI, placebo MDI, Ventolin Evohaler 3–7 day washout between periods; FEV₁ as primary endpoint Tacrine for Alzheimer's disease Peace & Koch, Biometrics 1993 Placebo, tacrine 40 mg/day, tacrine 80 mg/day Sequences restricted for safety so the higher dose never preceded the lower — balance deliberately sacrificed to clinical constraint BADGER — paediatric asthma step-up NCT00395304 (Lemanske et al., NEJM 2010) LABA step-up, ICS step-up, LTRA step-up Each child received all three therapies; LABA was most often best at the population level, but many individual children responded best to ICS or LTRA — heterogeneity a parallel design would have hidden Two periods, four sequences. The same-treatment arms (AA, BB) let you estimate the direct treatment effect and the carryover effect consistently — the alternative route to the problem multi-period designs solve. Figure 13: Balaam’s design (AA / AB / BA / BB). A montelukast trial in perennial allergic rhinitis ( Allergy Asthma Proc , 2008) used this structure to assess nasal congestion and sleep disturbance against placebo, with the same-treatment sequences supporting formal carryover estimation. 8 Summary Multi-crossover designs extend the standard crossover into something considerably more informative: treatment-specific within-subject variances, carryover that can be estimated rather than assumed away, more than two treatments at once, and real tolerance of dropout. That comes at a price — longer trials, harder logistics, more demanding assumptions, and a persistent risk of carryover and functional unblinding. Use them when the assumptions are genuinely defensible, not merely convenient. Table 13: Multi-crossover designs at a glance.
